claim: The diaphragm muscle is essential for breathing in mammals.
source: The diaphragm muscle is essential for breathing in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mammalian respiratory physiology.

claim: The diaphragm's asymmetric elevation during contraction correlates with morphological features suggestive of inherent left–right (L/R) asymmetry.
source: Its asymmetric elevation during contraction correlates with morphological features suggestive of inherent left–right (L/R) asymmetry.
evidence: This statement is presented as an observation that motivates the study, drawing on existing knowledge of diaphragm function.

claim: Both the diaphragm muscle and phrenic nerves have asymmetries, which can be established independently of each other during early embryogenesis.
source: Here, we have combined the analysis of genetically modified mouse models with transcriptomic analysis to show that both the diaphragm muscle and phrenic nerves have asymmetries, which can be established independently of each other during early embryogenesis in pathway instructed by Nodal, a morphogen that also conveys asymmetry in other organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetically modified mouse models and transcriptomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Diaphragm muscle and phrenic nerve asymmetries are established in a pathway instructed by Nodal.
source: Here, we have combined the analysis of genetically modified mouse models with transcriptomic analysis to show that both the diaphragm muscle and phrenic nerves have asymmetries, which can be established independently of each other during early embryogenesis in pathway instructed by Nodal, a morphogen that also conveys asymmetry in other organs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Nodal pathway mutants (Pitx2 and Rfx3) showing loss of asymmetries.

claim: Nodal is a morphogen that conveys asymmetry in other organs.
source: Here, we have combined the analysis of genetically modified mouse models with transcriptomic analysis to show that both the diaphragm muscle and phrenic nerves have asymmetries, which can be established independently of each other during early embryogenesis in pathway instructed by Nodal, a morphogen that also conveys asymmetry in other organs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Nodal signaling in developmental biology.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons receive an early L/R genetic imprint.
source: We further found that phrenic motoneurons receive an early L/R genetic imprint, with L versus R differences both in Slit/Robo signaling and MMP2 activity and in the contribution of both pathways to establish phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic data showing differential gene expression and protein activity between left and right motoneurons.

claim: There are L versus R differences in Slit/Robo signaling in phrenic motoneurons.
source: We further found that phrenic motoneurons receive an early L/R genetic imprint, with L versus R differences both in Slit/Robo signaling and MMP2 activity and in the contribution of both pathways to establish phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing differential Robo1 protein forms between left and right motoneurons.

claim: There are L versus R differences in MMP2 activity in phrenic motoneurons.
source: We further found that phrenic motoneurons receive an early L/R genetic imprint, with L versus R differences both in Slit/Robo signaling and MMP2 activity and in the contribution of both pathways to establish phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by in situ zymography data showing higher gelatinase activity in right motoneurons.

claim: Both Slit/Robo signaling and MMP2 activity contribute to establish phrenic nerve asymmetry.
source: We further found that phrenic motoneurons receive an early L/R genetic imprint, with L versus R differences both in Slit/Robo signaling and MMP2 activity and in the contribution of both pathways to establish phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by genetic loss-of-function experiments in Robo1/2 and Mmp2 mutants showing altered nerve patterns.

claim: Many diseases, including congenital hernia, degenerative pathologies and spinal cord injury, affect diaphragm function and thereby cause morbidity and mortality.
source: Many diseases, including congenital hernia, degenerative pathologies and spinal cord injury, affect diaphragm function and thereby cause morbidity and mortality (Greer, 2013; McCool and Tzelepis, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: L/R asymmetries in diaphragm morphology and contraction were inferred to be simply an adaptation to the structure of other, surrounding asymmetric organs such as the lungs.
source: Despite the large interest given to diaphragm function in various physiological and pathological contexts (Lin et al., 2000; Misgeld et al., 2002; Strochlic et al., 2012), little attention has been paid to the embryological origin of left–right (L/R) asymmetries in diaphragm morphology and contraction, in part because they were inferred to be simply an adaptation to the structure of other, surrounding asymmetric organs such as the lungs (Laskowski et al., 1991; Whitelaw, 1987).
evidence: This describes a previous hypothesis in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons arise in the spinal cord at cervical levels C3 to C5.
source: In the present study, we investigated the origin and the mechanisms responsible for the establishment of the diaphragm asymmetries, including motor innervation by the left and right phrenic motoneurons that arise in the spinal cord at cervical levels C3 to C5 (Greer et al., 1999; Laskowski and Owens, 1994).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many L/R asymmetries are determined prenatally.
source: As many L/R asymmetries are determined prenatally (Sun et al., 2005), we analyzed the diaphragm innervation of mouse embryos on embryonic day (E) 15.5, when synaptic contacts begin to be established in this organ (Lin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic contacts begin to be established in the diaphragm at E15.5.
source: As many L/R asymmetries are determined prenatally (Sun et al., 2005), we analyzed the diaphragm innervation of mouse embryos on embryonic day (E) 15.5, when synaptic contacts begin to be established in this organ (Lin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The phrenic nerves split into primary dorsal and ventral branches when reaching the lateral muscles at E15.5.
source: We observed that the phrenic nerves split into primary dorsal and ventral branches when reaching the lateral muscles, whereby the distance from the end-plate to the nerve entry point differs between the left and right side and results in a characteristic 'T' -like pattern on the left and 'V' -like pattern on the right (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by neurofilament staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The distance from the end-plate to the nerve entry point differs between the left and right side of the diaphragm.
source: We observed that the phrenic nerves split into primary dorsal and ventral branches when reaching the lateral muscles, whereby the distance from the end-plate to the nerve entry point differs between the left and right side and results in a characteristic 'T' -like pattern on the left and 'V' -like pattern on the right (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The left phrenic nerve exhibits a characteristic 'T'-like pattern.
source: We observed that the phrenic nerves split into primary dorsal and ventral branches when reaching the lateral muscles, whereby the distance from the end-plate to the nerve entry point differs between the left and right side and results in a characteristic 'T' -like pattern on the left and 'V' -like pattern on the right (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by visual data in Figure 1A.

claim: The right phrenic nerve exhibits a characteristic 'V'-like pattern.
source: We observed that the phrenic nerves split into primary dorsal and ventral branches when reaching the lateral muscles, whereby the distance from the end-plate to the nerve entry point differs between the left and right side and results in a characteristic 'T' -like pattern on the left and 'V' -like pattern on the right (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by visual data in Figure 1A.

claim: Similar differences in the L/R branching patterns are present in the human diaphragm.
source: Similar differences in the L/R branching patterns are present in the human diaphragm (Hidayet et al., 1974) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reproduced figure.

claim: There is an asymmetric number of branches defasciculating from the left and right primary nerves to innervate the motor end-plates.
source: Additionally, we observed an asymmetric number of branches defasciculating from the left and right primary nerves to innervate the motor end-plates (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The L/R distribution of acetylcholine receptor (AchR) clusters at the nascent neuromuscular junctions differs, with a 2.1 ± 0.2-fold increase in the medio-lateral scattering of AchR clusters on the right side of the diaphragm compared to the left side.
source: We further found that the L/R distribution of acetylcholine receptor (AchR) clusters at the nascent neuromuscular junctions also differed, with a 2.1 ± 0.2-fold increase in the medio-lateral scattering of AchR clusters on the right side of the diaphragm compared to the left side (N = 11, p<0.001 Wilcoxon) (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative bungarotoxin staining data with statistical analysis.

claim: Asymmetric nerve patterns arose at E12.5, concomitantly with branch formation.
source: The time course analysis revealed that these asymmetric nerve patterns arose at E12.5, concomitantly with branch formation (Figure 1C–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by time course imaging data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Phrenic branch patterns exhibit clear asymmetries before synapse formation and fetal respiratory movements.
source: Thus, phrenic branch patterns exhibit clear asymmetries before synapse formation and fetal respiratory movements (Lin et al., 2001, 2008), and are therefore unlikely to be induced by nerve activity or muscle contraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing data and citations about when synapse formation and respiratory movements occur.

claim: Phrenic nerve asymmetries are unlikely to be induced by nerve activity or muscle contraction.
source: Thus, phrenic branch patterns exhibit clear asymmetries before synapse formation and fetal respiratory movements (Lin et al., 2001, 2008), and are therefore unlikely to be induced by nerve activity or muscle contraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of events.

claim: Nodal signaling initiates a left-restricted transcriptional cascade to establish visceral asymmetry.
source: We therefore asked whether diaphragm nerve asymmetry was genetically hard-wired downstream of Nodal signaling, which initiates a left-restricted transcriptional cascade to establish visceral asymmetry (Komatsu and Mishina, 2013; Nakamura and Hamada, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PITX2C is a transcription factor downstream of Nodal.
source: First, we examined Pitx2∆C/∆C embryos lacking PITX2C, a transcription factor downstream of Nodal (Essner et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2001; Schweickert et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of PITX2C, Nodal signaling is interrupted, which causes a right pulmonary isomerism.
source: In the absence of PITX2C, Nodal signaling is interrupted, which causes a right pulmonary isomerism (i.e. the left lung has three main lobes like the right lung, instead of only one) (Liu et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on Pitx2 mutants.

claim: RFX3 is essential for cilia function that helps to distribute Nodal to the left side of the body.
source: Second, we examined Rfx3–/– embryos lacking RFX3, which is essential for cilia function that helps to distribute Nodal to the left side of the body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RFX3 function.

claim: Some Rfx3–/– embryos exhibit bilateral Nodal expression and left pulmonary isomerism.
source: As a result, some Rfx3–/– embryos exhibit bilateral Nodal expression and left pulmonary isomerism (i.e. the right lung has one lobe like the left lung) (Bonnafe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Diaphragm L/R nerve asymmetries were lost in both Pitx2∆C/∆C and Rfx3–/– embryos with impaired visceral asymmetries at E14.5.
source: We found that diaphragm L/R nerve asymmetries were lost in both Pitx2∆C/∆C and Rfx3–/– embryos with impaired visceral asymmetries at E14.5 (Figure 2A–E) (number of secondary branches, Wt versus mutant with lung isomerism: PITX2C, p=4.493E-5; RFX3, p=0.002884; defasciculation distance, Wt versus mutant with lung isomerism: PITX2C, p=0.001268; RFX3, p=2.719E-6, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of nerve patterns in mutant embryos shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Nodal pathway is essential for the establishment of diaphragm nerve asymmetry.
source: Thus, the Nodal pathway is essential for the establishment of diaphragm nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments with Nodal pathway mutants.

claim: In 2/10 Pitx2∆C/∆C embryos, nerve patterns were normal even though the lungs were isomerized.
source: However, the analysis of Pitx2∆C/∆C and Rfx3–/– mutants showed that the pattern of nerve asymmetry did not always correlate with the pattern of lung asymmetry; for example, in 2/10 Pitx2∆C/∆C embryos, nerve patterns were normal even though the lungs were isomerized (20%; Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of individual embryos shown in Figure 3.

claim: 1/13 Rfx3–/– embryos exhibited nerve isomerism together with pulmonary situs inversus.
source: Moreover, 1/13 Rfx3–/– embryos exhibited nerve isomerism together with pulmonary situs inversus, and nerve patterns were reversed in 1/13 embryo with lung isomerism (7.7% and 7.7%; Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual embryos shown in Figure 3.

claim: L/R asymmetry of the lateral diaphragm muscles was lost in both Pitx2∆C/∆C and Rfx3–/– mutants.
source: Alternatively, it is conceivable that muscle asymmetry controls nerve asymmetry. In agreement with this possibility, L/R asymmetry of the lateral diaphragm muscles was lost in both Pitx2∆C/∆C and Rfx3–/– mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by visual and quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Muscle width did not correlate with changes in nerve patterns in 2/10 Pitx2∆C/∆C embryos or in 6/13 Rfx3–/– embryos.
source: However, muscle width did not correlate with changes in nerve patterns in 2/10 Pitx2∆C/∆C embryos or in 6/13 Rfx3–/– embryos (20% and 46.2%, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual embryos.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons possess intrinsic L/R differences that are established independently of visceral and muscle asymmetries.
source: Together, these findings raise the possibility that phrenic motoneurons possess intrinsic L/R differences that are established independently of visceral and muscle asymmetries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uncoupling of nerve, lung, and muscle asymmetries observed in mutants.

claim: 3D reconstructions of cervical spinal cord tissue immunolabeled with Pou3f1/Oct6 did not reveal any obvious differences in the L/R organization of the cervical motoneuron pools in the spinal cord.
source: 3D reconstructions of cervical spinal cord tissue immunolabeled with Pou3f1/Oct6, whose expression has been reported in motoneurons (Philippidou et al., 2012), did not reveal any obvious differences in the L/R organization of the cervical motoneuron pools in the spinal cord (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Pou3f1/Oct6 expression has been reported in motoneurons.
source: 3D reconstructions of cervical spinal cord tissue immunolabeled with Pou3f1/Oct6, whose expression has been reported in motoneurons (Philippidou et al., 2012), did not reveal any obvious differences in the L/R organization of the cervical motoneuron pools in the spinal cord (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Axons explanted from right tissue extended over longer distances and were organized differently than axons explanted from left tissue.
source: We observed that axons explanted from right tissue extended over longer distances and were organized differently than axons explanted from left tissue (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of explant cultures shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Intrinsic factors present within the ventral spinal cord confer different behaviors to left and right motoneuron axons.
source: This observation suggests that intrinsic factors present within the ventral spinal cord confer different behaviors to left and right motoneuron axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the explant culture data.

claim: Among 22,600 transcripts expressed above background, 146 were enriched on the left and 194 on the right.
source: We further observed that amongst 22,600 transcripts expressed above background, 146 were enriched on the left and 194 on the right, with a predominance of transcripts encoding nuclear proteins (differentially enriched transcripts: right 35.56% versus left 26.02%; Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: There is a predominance of transcripts encoding nuclear proteins among differentially enriched transcripts (right 35.56% versus left 26.02%).
source: We further observed that amongst 22,600 transcripts expressed above background, 146 were enriched on the left and 194 on the right, with a predominance of transcripts encoding nuclear proteins (differentially enriched transcripts: right 35.56% versus left 26.02%; Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of microarray data.

claim: Morf4l1 protein was enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.81 ± 0.163, p=0.0022).
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that Morf4l1, a protein involved in histone acetylation/deacetylation and chromatin remodeling and reported to be essential for neural precursor proliferation and differentiation (Chen et al., 2009; Boije et al., 2013), was enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.81 ± 0.163, p=0.0022, Mann-Whitney; Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Morf4l1 is a protein involved in histone acetylation/deacetylation and chromatin remodeling and is essential for neural precursor proliferation and differentiation.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that Morf4l1, a protein involved in histone acetylation/deacetylation and chromatin remodeling and reported to be essential for neural precursor proliferation and differentiation (Chen et al., 2009; Boije et al., 2013), was enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.81 ± 0.163, p=0.0022, Mann-Whitney; Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Xrn2 was enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.37 ± 0.13, p=0.028).
source: Xrn2, a protein regulating RNA processing and miR stability that regulates miR expression in neurons (Kinjo et al., 2013), was also enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.37 ± 0.13, p=0.028; Mann-Whitney; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Xrn2 is a protein regulating RNA processing and miR stability that regulates miR expression in neurons.
source: Xrn2, a protein regulating RNA processing and miR stability that regulates miR expression in neurons (Kinjo et al., 2013), was also enriched in the left cervical motoneuron domain (L/R fold-change 1.37 ± 0.13, p=0.028; Mann-Whitney; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cervical motoneurons are intrinsically L/R-specified.
source: Thus, cervical motoneurons are intrinsically L/R-specified.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptomic and protein expression data.

claim: Slit/Robo signaling controls phrenic axon fasciculation.
source: To determine whether molecular differences in L/R specification manifest themselves in differential axon guidance responses, we studied mice lacking Slit/Robo signaling, which is known to regulate the fasciculation of phrenic axons (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Robo1–/–;Robo2–/– double mutants exhibit defective nerve defasciculation.
source: In agreement with prior reports, we observed defective nerve defasciculation in Robo1–/–;Robo2–/– double mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In Robo1–/–;Robo2–/– double mutants, defasciculation of the left nerve was as high as that of the right nerve and assumed a similar pattern in the left and right diaphragm.
source: Notably, defasciculation of the left nerve was as high as that of the right nerve and assumed a similar pattern in the left and right diaphragm, rather than adopting the normal asymmetric pattern seen in wild-type littermates (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Partial symmetrization was observed in double heterozygous mutants, indicating concentration-dependent sensitivity of phrenic nerve axons to Slit signals.
source: Partial symmetrization was observed in double heterozygous mutants, indicating concentration-dependent sensitivity of phrenic nerve axons to Slit signals (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of heterozygous mutants shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is no evidence for lateralized expression of the transcripts for Robo1 or the ligands of Robo1: Slit1, Slit2 and Slit3.
source: To determine whether differential levels of Slit/Robo signaling dictate the L/R pattern of phrenic nerve fasciculation, we examined their transcript levels, but found no evidence for lateralized expression of the transcripts for Robo1, the major regulator of diaphragm innervation (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012), or the ligands of Robo1: Slit1, Slit2 and Slit3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Robo1 is the major regulator of diaphragm innervation.
source: To determine whether differential levels of Slit/Robo signaling dictate the L/R pattern of phrenic nerve fasciculation, we examined their transcript levels, but found no evidence for lateralized expression of the transcripts for Robo1, the major regulator of diaphragm innervation (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012), or the ligands of Robo1: Slit1, Slit2 and Slit3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: L/R differences in Robo1 protein were identified by immunoblotting of phrenic motor neuron-enriched cervical spinal cord tissue.
source: By contrast, we identified L/R differences in Robo1 protein by immunoblotting of phrenic motor neuron-enriched cervical spinal cord tissue.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Robo1 was detected in one long and two short forms.
source: Robo1 was detected in one long and two short forms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereby the long Robo1 form migrating as a 250 kDa protein was enriched in the left samples and the short forms migrating as 120 kDa and 130 kDa proteins were enriched in the right samples (R/L ratio— 1.22 ± 0.1, p=0.01587; Mann-Whitney, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The long Robo1 form migrating as a 250 kDa protein was enriched in the left samples.
source: Robo1 was detected in one long and two short forms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereby the long Robo1 form migrating as a 250 kDa protein was enriched in the left samples and the short forms migrating as 120 kDa and 130 kDa proteins were enriched in the right samples (R/L ratio— 1.22 ± 0.1, p=0.01587; Mann-Whitney, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The short Robo1 forms migrating as 120 kDa and 130 kDa proteins were enriched in the right samples (R/L ratio— 1.22 ± 0.1, p=0.01587).
source: Robo1 was detected in one long and two short forms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereby the long Robo1 form migrating as a 250 kDa protein was enriched in the left samples and the short forms migrating as 120 kDa and 130 kDa proteins were enriched in the right samples (R/L ratio— 1.22 ± 0.1, p=0.01587; Mann-Whitney, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both human and drosophila Robo1 have been shown to be processed by metalloproteases.
source: However, both human and drosophila Robo1 have been shown to be processed by metalloproteases (Seki et al., 2010; Coleman et al., 2010), and potential cleavage fragments have been reported in mouse brain tissues (Clark et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Potential cleavage fragments of Robo1 have been reported in mouse brain tissues.
source: However, both human and drosophila Robo1 have been shown to be processed by metalloproteases (Seki et al., 2010; Coleman et al., 2010), and potential cleavage fragments have been reported in mouse brain tissues (Clark et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Differential post-translation processing of Robo proteins may be involved in creating L/R asymmetries in diaphragm innervations.
source: These findings raise the possibility that differential post-translation processing of Robo proteins may be involved in creating L/R asymmetries in diaphragm innervations.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differential Robo1 forms and literature on Robo processing.

claim: Metalloproteases have emerged as important regulators of axonal behaviors during development and regeneration.
source: Given that metalloproteases have emerged as important regulators of axonal behaviors during development and regeneration (Bai and Pfaff, 2011; Łukaszewicz-Zając et al., 2014; Small and Crawford, 2016; Verslegers et al., 2013b), we concentrated on these effectors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cervical motoneurons express several metalloproteases.
source: Consistent with previous expression data (GSE41013) (Philippidou et al., 2012), our transcriptome analysis indicated that cervical motoneurons express several metalloproteases.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and citation to previous expression data.

claim: Among the 7 Mmps and 13 ADAMs expressed by cervical motoneurons, Mmp2 and ADAM17 were expressed at higher levels in the right motoneurons.
source: Interestingly, among the 7 Mmps and 13 ADAMs expressed by cervical motoneurons, Mmp2 and ADAM17 were expressed at higher levels in the right motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: MMP2 controls axon development in mouse and motor axon fasciculation in drosophila.
source: We focused on MMP2 because it was shown to control axon development in mouse and motor axon fasciculation in drosophila (Miller et al., 2011; Gaublomme et al., 2014; Zuo et al., 1998; Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mmp2 transcripts were enriched in the Hb9-positive right motoneurons.
source: The microarray analysis showed that Mmp2 transcripts were enriched in the Hb9-positive right motoneurons, which was confirmed using qRT-PCR and quantitative in situ hybridization (log2(R/L) Embryo 1 — 0.22 ± 0.08; Embryo 2 — 0.63 ± 0.11, RNAscope) (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by microarray, qRT-PCR, and RNAscope data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Gelatinase activity on the axon shaft and growth cones was 1.6 times higher in right than in left motoneuron cultures.
source: Moreover, in situ zymography with DQ-Gelatin (Hill et al., 2012), which is effectively cleaved by MMP2 (Snoek-van Beurden and Von den Hoff, 2005), showed that gelatinase activity on the axon shaft and growth cones was 1.6 times higher in right than in left motoneuron cultures (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ zymography data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DQ-Gelatin is effectively cleaved by MMP2.
source: Moreover, in situ zymography with DQ-Gelatin (Hill et al., 2012), which is effectively cleaved by MMP2 (Snoek-van Beurden and Von den Hoff, 2005), showed that gelatinase activity on the axon shaft and growth cones was 1.6 times higher in right than in left motoneuron cultures (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The differential L/R MMP activity was absent in motoneuron cultures prepared from Rfx3–/– embryos with phenotypic left isomerism.
source: Remarkably, this difference was absent in motoneuron cultures prepared from Rfx3–/– embryos with phenotypic left isomerism (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ zymography data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The differential L/R MMP activity is controlled by the Nodal pathway.
source: These results provide evidence that the differential L/R MMP activity is controlled by the Nodal pathway and further suggest that MMP2 contributes to the establishment of phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of differential MMP activity in Rfx3 mutants.

claim: MMP2 contributes to the establishment of phrenic nerve asymmetry.
source: These results provide evidence that the differential L/R MMP activity is controlled by the Nodal pathway and further suggest that MMP2 contributes to the establishment of phrenic nerve asymmetry.
evidence: This is suggested by the differential MMP2 expression and activity data.

claim: At E14.5, Mmp2–/– embryos exhibited normal lung asymmetry and well-developed phrenic branches on both sides.
source: At E14.5, Mmp2–/– embryos exhibited normal lung asymmetry and well-developed phrenic branches on both sides (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: E14.5 Mmp2–/– embryos exhibited a partial symmetrization of the phrenic branches, with a right pattern that resembled the one observed on the left in control littermates.
source: Interestingly, we observed a partial symmetrization of the phrenic branches, with a right pattern that resembled the one observed on the left in control littermates in E14.5 Mmp2–/– embryos (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Higher right MMP2 activity could contribute to promote the right pattern of phrenic nerve defasciculation.
source: Thus, higher right MMP2 activity could contribute to promote the right pattern of phrenic nerve defasciculation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Mmp2 mutant phenotype.

claim: The first asymmetry instruction in diaphragm patterning is provided by early Nodal signaling.
source: Taken together, our work shows that the first asymmetry instruction in diaphragm patterning is provided by early Nodal signaling, which sets the L/R axis and visceral asymmetry of the embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments with Nodal pathway mutants.

claim: Phrenic motoneurons have an intrinsic, genetically encoded L/R asymmetry that manifests itself in the differential activation of molecules that have key roles in axon guidance, including Robo1 and MMP2.
source: Beyond this early mechanism, phrenic motoneurons have an intrinsic, genetically encoded L/R asymmetry that manifests itself in the differential activation of molecules that have key roles in axon guidance, including Robo1 and MMP2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptomic, protein expression, and functional data.

claim: Lefty expression in the prospective floor plate of the neural tube prevents Nodal diffusion to the left LPM.
source: In agreement with this idea, it has been suggested that Lefty expression in the prospective floor plate of the neural tube prevents Nodal diffusion to the left LPM (Shiratori and Hamada, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lefty expression is confined to the left prospective floor plate and is reversed or expanded bilaterally in 'iv' or 'inv' mutants.
source: Moreover, Lefty expression is confined to the left prospective floor plate and is reversed or expanded bilaterally in 'iv' or 'inv' mutants, which exhibit reverse visceral asymmetry (Meno et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The floor plate has a key role in the patterning and specification of spinal cord neuronal lineages.
source: Given the key role of the floor plate in the patterning and specification of spinal cord neuronal lineages (Goulding et al., 1993; Placzek et al., 1991), left and right floor plate cells might also differently imprint left and right spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cells invading the ventral spinal cord exhibit L/R asymmetries that can be preserved during their migration.
source: Alternatively, or additionally, endothelial cells invading the ventral spinal cord could convey early Nodal signaling from the LPM to the spinal cord. Indeed, these cells exhibit L/R asymmetries that can be preserved during their migration (Chi et al., 2003; Klessinger and Christ, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In zebrafish habenula, differences in both the timing of neurogenesis and exposure to lateralized signal during neuron differentiation act in parallel to set L/R asymmetries.
source: Indeed, recent work in zebrafish habenula suggests that differences in both the timing of neurogenesis and exposure to lateralized signal during neuron differentiation act in parallel to set L/R asymmetries (Hüsken et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Early imprinting of progenitors in Caenorhabditis elegans induces an epigenetic mark for L/R identity that drives differential genetic programs during neuron differentiation.
source: Interestingly, early imprinting of progenitors in Caenorhabditis elegans induces an epigenetic mark for L/R identity that drives differential genetic programs during neuron differentiation (Cochella and Hobert, 2012; O'Meara et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Slit/Robo signaling controls phrenic axon fasciculation.
source: For example, we found that Slit/Robo signaling is required for the establishment of asymmetric nerve patterns, which suggests that left and right phrenic motoneurons have different Slit/Robo signaling levels. Interestingly, Slit/Robo signaling has previously been shown to control phrenic axon fasciculation (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In drosophila, cleavage of Robo by ADAM10 is required for recruitment of downstream signaling molecules and the axon guidance response.
source: In drosophila, cleavage of Robo by ADAM10 is required for recruitment of downstream signaling molecules and the axon guidance response (Coleman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Metalloproteases can decrease the amount of available receptors and/or terminate adhesion and signaling.
source: Metalloproteases can also decrease the amount of available receptors and/or terminate adhesion and signaling (Bai and Pfaff, 2011; Hinkle et al., 2006; Romi et al., 2014; Hattori et al., 2000; Gatto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MMP2 controls motor axon fasciculation in drosophila.
source: We focused on MMP2 because it was shown to control axon development in mouse and motor axon fasciculation in drosophila (Miller et al., 2011; Gaublomme et al., 2014; Zuo et al., 1998; Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteomic studies have identified more than 40 secreted and transmembrane substrates for MMP2.
source: For example, proteomic studies have identified more than 40 secreted and transmembrane substrates for MMP2 (Dean and Overall, 2007), of which we found 32 to be expressed in cervical motoneurons including Adam17, which is enriched in right motoneurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: 32 MMP2 substrates are expressed in cervical motoneurons including Adam17, which is enriched in right motoneurons.
source: For example, proteomic studies have identified more than 40 secreted and transmembrane substrates for MMP2 (Dean and Overall, 2007), of which we found 32 to be expressed in cervical motoneurons including Adam17, which is enriched in right motoneurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Cleavage of human Robo1 has been suggested to be MMP-dependent.
source: First, cleavage of human Robo1 has been suggested to be MMP-dependent, although in drosophila, Robo1 is cleaved by Adam10/Kuzbanian (Coleman et al., 2010; Seki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In drosophila, Robo1 is cleaved by Adam10/Kuzbanian.
source: First, cleavage of human Robo1 has been suggested to be MMP-dependent, although in drosophila, Robo1 is cleaved by Adam10/Kuzbanian (Coleman et al., 2010; Seki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Incubation of cervical spinal cord tissue with active MMP2 significantly increased the short Robo1 forms (fold change: 1.60 ± 0.23, p=0.00285).
source: In support, incubation of cervical spinal cord tissue with active MMP2 significantly increased the short Robo1 forms (fold change: 1.60 ± 0.23, p=0.00285, Mann-Whitney, four independent western blots, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: NCAM is highly expressed by developing phrenic axons, controls axon-axon fasciculation, and is cleaved by MMPs.
source: An additional MMP candidate is NCAM, which is highly expressed by developing phrenic axons, controls axon-axon fasciculation, and is cleaved by MMPs (Dean and Overall, 2007; Hinkle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Right-sided fetal forelimb movements are far more frequent than left-sided movements at developmental stages when motoneurons have not yet received any input from higher brain centers.
source: For example, the L/R imprinting of spinal motoneuron might also explain why right-sided fetal forelimb movements are far more frequent than left-sided movements at developmental stages when motoneurons have not yet received any input from higher brain centers (Hepper et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Congenital hernias generally affect the left hemi-diaphragm and can cause perinatal lethality.
source: Examples include congenital hernias, which generally affect the left hemi-diaphragm and can cause perinatal lethality (Pober, 2008), and some types of congenital myopathies that impair diaphragm function only on one side (Grogan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Some types of congenital myopathies impair diaphragm function only on one side.
source: Examples include congenital hernias, which generally affect the left hemi-diaphragm and can cause perinatal lethality (Pober, 2008), and some types of congenital myopathies that impair diaphragm function only on one side (Grogan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.
